newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: FISCHER SAYS TAX REFORM ON COALITION'S AGENDA
The Deputy Prime Minister, Tim Fischer, says tax reform is part of the unfinished business on the Government's agenda of the 1990s.
While the Prime Minister has promised not to introduce a Goods and Services tax in his first term, the possibility of such a reform is likely if the Coalition gains a second term.
Tim Fischer, says the Coalition has learned a lot about how to manage the debate on tax reform, and has echoed John Howard's comments that the present system needs to be overhauled.
Mr Fischer led the National Party in 1993 when voters rejected a GST, and says the Coalition learned a lot from that experience.
BORBIDGE: FISCHER'S BARGAINING POWER NOT STRONG
Queensland Premier, Rob Borbidge, says National Party leader, Tim Fischer, has limited bargaining power with the Prime Minister.
Mr Borbidge has come to the defence of the embattled Deputy Prime Minister, who's come under fire from party members, and some backbenchers, for backing the Prime Minister's native title plan.
Mr Borbidge, who has been among Mr Fischer's critics, says John Howard could lead a majority government without the help of the Nationals.
He says this means Mr Fischer is Deputy Prime Minister by invitation only, which dilutes his bargaining power on issues like native title.
LABOR MAKING ITS POSITION ON GST CLEAR
The Federal Opposition has moved to make its position clear on a Goods and Services Tax following differing opinions put forward by the Labor leader and the Shadow Treasurer.
Earlier today, Gareth Evans told ABC radio that the ALP would support an equitable GST, but Kim Beazley says the remarks were taken out of context.
Mr Beazley says he's sure Mr Evans was dismissive of the notion that a GST could ever be made equitable.
He says Labor's position is that a GST is not needed in Australia.
Mr Beazley says a GST is an inflationary tax, wouldn't bring down the tax burden on middle Australia, wouldn't create jobs, and would be hard on small business.
GOVT DENIES ROLE IN REPORT INTO ABORTION SERVICES
The Federal Government's denied any role in delaying the release of a major report into abortion services.

The report by the National Health and Medical Research Council recommends greater access to the morning-after pill, more testing on the banned French abortion pill RU-486, and a travel allowance for rural women seeking abortions.

Professor John Funder who missed out on the job as Council President, has accused the government of delaying the report's release because of pressure from the anti-abortion lobby, including Independent Senator Brian Harradine.
But a spokesman for Health Minister Michael Wooldridge says the delay has nothing to do with the government.
He says the report's findings were at odds with the Council's earlier position on abortion, and the Council will release the report in two weeks, once its logo is removed from the cover.
CALL FOR SPECIAL BRANCH FILES TO BE RELEASED
In New South Wales, a senior official from the disgraced and now disbanded police Special Branch unit has backed calls for its files to be released.
The unit was shut down earlier this year when the Police Royal Commission heard evidence that it had been keeping files on certain activitists, lawyers and politicians.
Civil liberties groups have called for the Special Branch files to be released.
John Garvey was a member of the unit and was also a casualty of the Royal Commission on an unrelated matter.
But he says it's time for the files to be turned over to interested parties.
SOCCER: TOP SIDES MAY FACE EXPULSION

In soccer, Ericsson Cup teams South Melbourne and Sydney United will be charged with bringing the game into disrepute following fighting at the end of yesterday's preliminary final at Parramatta Stadium.
Soccer Australia officials will meet police tomorrow morning to investigate the fight and set up an inquiry.
If the charges are found to be proved, both clubs will be expelled from the national league competition.
Soccer Australia Chairman David Hill hopes the investigation will be completed within the next month.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
